title: Tariff Exposure Mapping: A Framework for Sub-Tier Supplier Visibility
summary: Tariff exposure mapping finds Section 232 risk hiding in sub-tier suppliers. Learn to build a repeatable framework tied to the BIS calendar.
body_markdown:
In this article, learn about:


-


Why Section 232 duties can reach manufacturers unexpectedly


-


The two mechanisms by which the covered product list changes


-


What a repeatable mapping framework requires, and who owns the refresh


---


Recent changes to Section 232 duties on steel, aluminum, and copper mean the tariffs now apply to a growing list of finished and semi-finished goods that contain those metals. As a result, a manufacturer can inherit real tariff costs through a part sourced two or three tiers upstream. That cost often surfaces as an unexplained price increase from a direct supplier, or as margin erosion at the finance close, rather than at the border.


This article lays out a repeatable framework for mapping that exposure: how to classify components by[Harmonized Tariff Schedule](https://hts.usitc.gov/) (HTS) code, how to trace which tier introduces each covered material, and how to tie the refresh to the regulatory calendar.


## What Is Tariff Exposure Mapping?


Tariff exposure mapping traces three things:


-


Which components contain tariff-covered materials


-


Which supplier tier brings each one in


-


What that exposure costs when duty rates move


Tariff exposure differs from standard customs classification by following the material.


The mechanism behind that difference is the HTS, which assigns every imported good a code at the border; what’s covered under Section 232 is defined by lists of those codes. When the U.S. Department of Commerce adds a derivative product to the steel or aluminum list, every import under that code becomes subject to duties.


A sub-tier supplier is the company that supplies goods to your supplier. Because each company imports under its own classifications, a covered component can enter the chain above your visibility and reach you inside a finished part, priced as an ordinary cost increase.


## Why Does Section 232 Tariff Exposure Keep Changing?


The covered list expands on a schedule, with two mechanisms widening it.


The first is the inclusions process that the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) runs on a fixed annual calendar. Companies may petition to add derivative products to the steel and aluminum tariffs during[three two-week windows each year](https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/commerce-department-opens-new-steel-and-aluminum-section-232-tariff-inclusions) , opening in January, May, and September. Each window is followed by a comment period and a decision within 60 days of the opening of that comment period.


Along with the fixed annual calendar, the broader U.S. Department of Commerce can propose additions, as it did in a[Federal Register notice published August 6, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/06/2026-15961/request-for-public-comments-on-the-proposed-implementation-of-duties-on-additional-aluminum-steel) seeking comment on 14 derivative categories and 20 HTS codes across steel, aluminum, and copper, at rates that vary by category. The comment period for that notice closed on August 27, 2026; the products named in that proposal are not subject to duties until the Secretary of Commerce issues a final determination adding them to the derivative list.


With two mechanisms running at once, the exposure picture can shift several times a year. A map finished in March may describe a different cost structure by October.


## How Is Sub-Tier Supplier Visibility?


[McKinsey’s 2025 supply chain risk survey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/operations/our-insights/supply-chain-risk-survey) of 100 companies found that 95% have visibility into tier-one supplier risks, while only 42% can see into tier two or beyond. In the same survey, 82% of respondents said new tariffs affect their supply chains.


Additionally, McKinsey reports that 58% have mapped their tier-two suppliers, but fewer than half of those companies keep regular direct contact with them.


Suppliers need both a completed tariff exposure map and a working relationship with their tier-two suppliers.


The map helps you understand your exposure to tariffs but can become outdated as tariffs change. An ongoing relationship with your tier-two suppliers, on the other hand, can help you catch changes such as when a supplier has changed its own sourcing between regulatory windows.


## How To Create a Repeatable Supply Chain Risk Mapping Framework


Multi-tier supply chain visibility becomes durable when the refresh is scheduled on a regular basis. Four components make the exercise repeatable.


### 1. Classify Components by HTS Code


The mapping unit is the component, because that is what the tariff lists address. Manufacturers that do this well hold an HTS code against each significant purchased part, including domestically bought parts, since a domestic supplier may be importing the subassembly it sells.


Classification is a legal determination, so most companies have customs counsel or a licensed broker to double-check it.


### 2. Trace Which Tier Introduces Each Covered Material


For every component carrying a covered classification, the question is where the steel, aluminum, or copper entered. Answering this requires information the vendor master does not hold, so this step usually runs as a structured request asking tier-one suppliers to identify their own sources for the parts in question. An unanswered request marks a component whose exposure is unknown rather than absent.


### 3. Tie the Refresh to the Regulatory Calendar


The BIS inclusion windows supply dates known in advance, which makes them a natural anchor for recurring review. A manufacturer working with that calendar should re-run classification when a window’s results publish and treat the comment periods as advance notice for components likely to be affected.


Proposals outside the petition calendar arrive without that lead time and should be handled as exceptions.


### 4. Name an Owner and a Reporting Line


Without a named owner, mapping will often happen once and then stop. The owner should sit in supply chain or trade compliance, and needs enough standing with tier-one suppliers that a request for sourcing information gets answered.


The owner’s findings go to finance as a cost figure: what share of a component’s price is tariff exposure. Finance decides whether to fund a response, whether that means requalifying a part, renegotiating a contract, or absorbing the cost.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Does tariff exposure mapping apply if we only buy from domestic suppliers?


Yes. A domestic supplier may import the components it sells, and Section 232 duties attach at that import regardless of where the final sale happens. Buying domestically changes who pays the duty, not whether the cost sits in the part price.


### How far up the chain do we need to map?


Far enough to reach the point where covered material enters, which varies by component. For a fabricated part that may be tier two; for an assembly it may be tier three or beyond. Most manufacturers prioritize by spend and by how close a classification sits to a covered code.


### Who should own the mapping process internally?


Supply chain or trade compliance typically owns the work, with a reporting line to finance for the cost view. The practical requirement is that the owner can ask tier-one suppliers for sourcing information and expect an answer.
